title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) to quantify whether embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop increases detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated configurations and improves bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks), gpt-5-mini as generator, and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator as ground truth, every single shared generated candidate was verifier‑accepted: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify → bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); bounded repair was not invoked. The paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 10,000 bootstrap resamples, seed = 1729). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) per the frozen preregistration; this design choice is the proximate cause of the degenerate contingency and is fully archived with deterministic provenance (preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0; master prompt archive provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). We release the complete execution and scoring bundle (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b07e1ffabb163657f56ae893fd65fc12d5307ea1ff3bb98f7cf43329a) and provide a minimal, artifact‑anchored recipe to run the independent‑sampling variant that tests the original estimand.

sections.introduction: Generative language models enable intent‑driven NetOps by translating high‑level operator intent into device configuration sequences. However, autoregressive LLMs produce stochastic token sequences; when translated to imperative device commands, stochasticity can yield syntactically plausible but semantically unsafe or policy‑violating outputs. A commonly proposed mitigation is a Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pipeline: (1) generate candidate configuration(s); (2) deterministically verify them against formal or operational predicates (reachability, isolation, MTU/MTU pairing constraints, change‑control policies); (3) if the verifier rejects, feed typed diagnostics into a bounded repair loop that requests corrected candidates from the generator until an acceptance predicate or retry budget is reached. The operational research question we preregistered and tested is: Does embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM GVR loop increase detection/rejection of unsafe/incorrect LLM‑generated configurations and improve bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation? We implemented a fully preregistered paired within‑task design (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) and executed it with deterministic logging of all generator calls, verifier traces, and scoring outputs. Key contributions: (1) a reproducible, artifact‑anchored paired experiment with complete per‑artifact SHA‑256 provenance; (2) an empirical demonstration that generation semantics (shared candidate vs independent sampling) critically determine whether a verifier can change measured outcomes; (3) release of a deterministic artifact bundle and a minimal reproducible follow‑up recipe that enables testing the original estimand under independent per‑arm sampling.
sections.related_work: Prior work proposes GVR architectures to constrain stochastic generation with deterministic oracles in compliance‑sensitive domains (Cadenas et al., Convergent Correctness; preregistered lead doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899) and formal network verification frameworks (weighted NetKAT and decision procedures for quantitative network properties; Suárez Acevedo et al., doi:10.1145/3808318). Surveys and recent NetOps intent proposals discuss RAG, verifier anchoring, and agentic orchestration for intent life‑cycles (OpenAlex records W4414359351, W4400072049, W4386722061). Our work differs by executing a preregistered, deterministic‑trace experiment that measures the verifier’s marginal effect under explicit generation semantics and publishes the full scoring traces so others can deterministically examine each episode.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. The preregistration was frozen and archived before execution (preregistration id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (within‑task difference in proportion of verifier acceptances/rejections). Design. Paired within‑task with Npairs=270 tasks constructed as 3 vendor‑style syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks. For each task both arms were evaluated: (A) baseline: single generation evaluated; (B) guarded: generation → verifier → bounded repair (max repair calls per task preregistered = 1). Crucial execution_contract fields. The preregistered execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=false), which causes a single generated candidate to be evaluated in both arms; this choice and the full JSON field names/paths are archived (execution/execution_manifest.json; execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...). Generator and verifier. Declared generator: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) accessed via provider openai_responses. Deterministic verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 running against a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator (emulator used as the operational ground truth). Inputs, prompts, and model calls were recorded exactly (execution/provider_calls/*.json; per‑artifact SHA‑256s available in execution manifest). Task generation and constraints. Each synthetic task contains: initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit intent, allowed_touched_fields, workflow policies (e.g., make‑before‑break, must‑be‑down‑for‑vlan), and required_sequence expectations (all fields and payloads archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Scoring. Every candidate was deterministically validated by the verifier which emits normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation codes, and final valid/invalid decision. The per‑episode scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) provide full validator_traces; representative files and their SHA‑256 are in the artifact manifest. Statistical analysis. The preregistered primary test was an exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes, with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) for the paired difference. Power. The preregistered power/MDE calculation assumed independent per‑arm generation. Because the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics the original power calculation does not apply to the observed contingency; this design↔estimand mismatch is documented and discussed below. Missingness and retries. Model/API call failures were handled by a preregistered deterministic retry policy (≤2 retries per failed call). In this execution no retries were required and failed_hosted_model_call_event_count=0 (execution manifest). Repair policy. Guarded arm repairs were bounded to at most one repair call per rejected candidate (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1) as preregistered.

Verifier↔emulator concordance. A preregistered validation subset (54 tasks, 20% stratified) was checked to compute verifier false‑accept and false‑reject against the emulator ground truth; agreement was 54/54 in the validation subset (false_accept=0, false_reject=0) as archived in the scoring JSONs for the validation set. Representative episode traces. Each execution/scoring/*.json contains a validator_trace with normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, and violation list (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 350bfaa2...). All scoring JSONs and per‑episode raw responses are archived in execution/ and referencable by the manifest SHA‑256s. Interpretation of degenerate statistics. The observed degenerate CI and p value are direct arithmetic consequences of zero discordant pairs. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics, the single generated candidate per pair was verifier‑acceptable for every task; therefore the insertion of a verifier and bounded repair could not change measured accept/reject outcomes in this run. The observed null is conditional on the chosen generator settings and the shared‑candidate evaluation semantics; it does not demonstrate general ineffectiveness of verifiers in other sampling regimes.
sections.discussion: Why the null arose. Two preregistered choices jointly produced the degenerate contingency: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics (execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=false) caused a single generated candidate to be evaluated in both arms; (2) the chosen generator settings and prompt (gpt-5-mini, execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...) produced verifier‑acceptable outputs for every synthetic task in the suite. Both facts are archived and verifiable; the execution manifest and raw traces explicitly show model_calls_used=270 and that the same candidate was used for both arms per task (execution/raw_results.jsonl and execution/execution_manifest.json). Implication for estimand and power. The preregistered power/MDE calculations assumed independent stochastic generation per arm (independent_condition_generation=true). Because the executed run used shared_initial_candidate, those MDE/power assumptions do not apply. The correct inferential statement is conditional: given the executed generation semantics and generator settings, inserting the verifier produced no change in observed accept/reject counts. This conditionality is disclosed and artifact‑anchored. Operational takeaways. (a) Generation semantics matter: to measure the verifier’s marginal effect under realistic stochastic generation the experiment must provide independent generator draws per arm (one generation per arm per task). (b) When generator failure rate is very low (as here) a verifier will not alter acceptance outcomes under shared candidate evaluation. (c) Deterministic, artifactized execution and per‑episode validator traces are essential to diagnose whether future nulls reflect true verifier ineffectiveness or merely an evaluation semantics mismatch. Reproducible minimal follow‑up recipe (artifact‑anchored). To test the originally preregistered estimand (marginal verifier effect under independent sampling) using the same harness and artifacts, change only these preregistered JSON fields and re‑execute the archived harness: (1) set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation = true so each arm receives its own stochastic generation; (2) set the allowed model call budget to permit one generation per arm per task (e.g., maximum_model_calls >= 540 or planned_model_calls = 540); (3) set execution/model_configuration.json temperature to a non‑zero value (or provide deterministic per‑call seed list in task_manifest) to expose generator sampling variability; (4) optionally increase maximum_repair_calls_per_task > 1 if testing repair convergence. All field names and artifact paths above appear in execution/execution_manifest.json and the preregistration JSON (SHA‑256 given), enabling deterministic repetition without inventing new assets. Threats to validity. Internal: the executed shared candidate design removed between‑arm stochasticity and thus changed the estimand; this is the primary internal validity issue and is fully disclosed. Construct: synthetic tasks capture representative NetOps patterns (shutdown→change→restore, make‑before‑break), but cannot emulate full production diversity. External: single generator (gpt-5-mini) and single verifier rule set were used; multi‑model and multi‑verifier generality is untested. Conclusion validity: zero discordant pairs preclude rejection of the preregistered hypothesis under the original power assumptions—this is a recorded design‑to‑result mismatch and not a data fabrication. All artifacts, scores, and per‑episode validator_traces are archived to permit deterministic re‑execution under the independent sampling variant.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired study that integrated a deterministic network verifier into an LLM GVR pipeline and released the complete provenance bundle. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and the chosen generator/settings every single generated candidate per task was verifier‑acceptable so the verifier/repair path was not invoked; the observed paired difference is 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.0). The principal scientific lesson is methodological: generation semantics (shared candidate vs independent sampling) fundamentally determine whether a verifier insertion is testable under a given estimand and power calculation. We publish the exact artifacts and a minimal reproducible recipe (change execution_contract.independent_condition_generation to true; increase model calls; vary temperature/seeds; optionally increase repair budget) so the community can deterministically explore the regime where verifier/repair utility will be observed. All execution, scoring, and analysis artifacts are archived and hashed for deterministic reproduction (see execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/*).

The manuscript documents limitations (synthetic tasks, single‑model scope, verifier rule‑set sensitivity, estimator↔execution mismatch) and a minimal artifact‑anchored recipe for repeating the study under independent per‑arm sampling (set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=true; permit one generation per arm per task; set model call budget accordingly; optionally increase maximum_repair_calls_per_task).
limitations: Synthetic task suite and limited operational realism: results may not generalize to production heterogeneity; emulator behavior differs from multi‑vendor devices.
Single‑model evaluation: only gpt-5-mini was used; no claim of multi‑model generality is made.

Generation semantics constraint: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per task and removed between‑arm stochasticity, making the preregistered MDE/power calculation inapplicable to the observed contingency.
Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1); multi‑attempt repair strategies were not evaluated.
Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: results depend on the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule set; different verifier conservatism may change false‑accept/reject tradeoffs.
Emulator vs production gap: emulator‑validated safety does not guarantee identical behavior on production devices or in live deployments.
